newsitem.title: GERMANY: German "Tony Blair" offers to make Kohl a "Major".
newsitem.headline: German "Tony Blair" offers to make Kohl a "Major".

text.p: A German cabaret artiste, lampooning Bonn's frantic search for its own "Tony Blair", offered himself on Friday to the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) as a challenger to veteran Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
"I'm young. I've never lost an election and I'm not an SPD party member. I think these credentials will win me credibility and support among the voters," said Robert Griess, 31.
"Let me be your Blair so that you can turn Kohl into a (former British prime minister John) Major."

Dressed in a dapper grey pinstripe suit, Griess told journalists at a Bonn cabaret theatre the SPD needed help from "outside" or would lose a fourth election in a row and pledged to transform it into Germany's answer to Blair's New Labour.

Germany's beleaguered opposition party plunged into soul-searching this week over whether they could find an equivalent to Blair, who led Britain's Labour to victory last week after 18 years in opposition.
The pro-business and media-friendly SPD Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder is seen by commentators and in opinion polls as a favourite to challenge Kohl.

But in contrast to Blair, Schroeder is an outsider in the SPD and could only run against Kohl with the agreement of SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine, who also has his sights on the top job despite losing to Kohl in 1990.
An SPD spokeswoman laughed off the artiste's offer, saying the party welcomed "all suggestions on how we can win the election and topple Kohl".
Griess declined to reveal any details of a possible election platform, saying he would have to discuss it with the party.
"Since the SPD cannot decide on a candidate from its own ranks, they should accept my offer," Griess said in a letter to the SPD headquarters in Bonn.

"With nearly four million unemployed, politics cannot be left solely to politicians. The commitment of every single individual is needed in a democracy -- just as the German president (Roman Herzog) says. From now on I no longer withhold my services," the letter said.
